question.:question/problem:
The temperature $T(t),$ in degrees Fahrenheit, of an exhaust pipe of a motorcycle can be modeled by the differential equation

$$
\frac{dT}{dt}=-0.16(T-74)
$$

where $t>0$ is the time, measured in minutes. If the initial temperature of the exhaust pipe is ${186}^{∘}F,$ calculate its temperature after $5$ minutes. Round your answer to the nearest integer.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We're told that the temperature of the exhaust pipe of a motorcycle is modeled by the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{dT}{dt}=-0.16(T-74).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-74} & =-0.16\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-74} & =-\int 0.16\,\text{d}t \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-74| & =-0.16t+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-74>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-74 & ={e}^{-0.16t+C} \\ T-74 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-0.16t} \\ T-74 & =K{e}^{-0.16t} \\ T & =74+K{e}^{-0.16t}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature of the exhaust pipe was ${186}^{∘}F.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=186,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}186 & =74+K{e}^{0} \\ 186 & =74+K \\ K & =112\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to our initial value problem is

$$
T(t)=74+112{e}^{-0.16t}.
$$

Finally, the temperature of the exhaust pipe after $t=5$ minutes is

$$
T(5)=74+112{e}^{-0.16\cdot 5}≈{124}^{∘}\text{F},
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-24).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-24} & =-k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-24} & =-k\int dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-24| & =-kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}T-24 & ={e}^{-kt+C} \\ T-24 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-kt} \\ T-24 & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =24+K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration.

$$
\begin{aligned}186 & =24+K{e}^{0} \\ 186 & =24+K \\ K & =162\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}{t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{4}{5} \right)}}{2}}\ln\left(\frac{11}{80\left(\frac{80}{64}\right)^{\frac{5}{2}}}\right) \\ {t}_{1} & =5+2\frac{\ln(\frac{11}{80})}{\ln(\frac{4}{5})}≈23\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

generation.domain: T(t)>ambient; positive rate; t>=0; observations strictly cooling

question.:question/problem: A heated metal body cools in a room at ${34}^{∘}\text{C}.$ Its temperature is ${86}^{∘}\text{C}$ after $1$ minute and ${63}^{∘}\text{C}$ after $5$ minutes. The temperature $T(t)$, in degrees Celsius, obeys Newton's law of cooling, with $t$ measured in minutes since cooling began. To the nearest minute, how long after cooling began does the body reach ${40}^{∘}\text{C}$?
question.:question/worked-solution:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-34),\qquad k>0.
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-34} & =-k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-34} & =-k\int dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-34| & =-kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-34>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-34 & ={e}^{-kt+C} \\ T-34 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-kt} \\ T-34 & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =34+K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

Apply the two observed conditions $T(1)=86$ and $T(5)=63$:

$$
\begin{aligned}86 & =34+Ke^{-1k} \\ 52 & =Ke^{-1k} \\ 63 & =34+Ke^{-5k} \\ 29 & =Ke^{-5k}\end{aligned}
$$

Divide the excess temperatures to eliminate $K$, then take natural logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{29}{52} & =\frac{Ke^{-5k}}{Ke^{-1k}} \\ \frac{29}{52} & =e^{-4k} \\ \ln(\frac{29}{52}) & =-4k \\ k & =- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{29}{52} \right)}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Now substitute this rate into $T(1)=86$ to determine the constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}52 & =Ke^{-1(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{29}{52} \right)}}{4})} \\ K & =52e^{1(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{29}{52} \right)}}{4})} \\ K & =52\left(\frac{52}{29}\right)^{\frac{1}{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution satisfying both observations is

$$
T(t)=34+52\left(\frac{52}{29}\right)^{\frac{1}{4}}e^{-(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{29}{52} \right)}}{4})t}.
$$

Substituting the two observation times confirms the model:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(1) & =34+(52\left(\frac{52}{29}\right)^{\frac{1}{4}})e^{-(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{29}{52} \right)}}{4})\cdot 1}=86 \\ T(5) & =34+(52\left(\frac{52}{29}\right)^{\frac{1}{4}})e^{-(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{29}{52} \right)}}{4})\cdot 5}=63\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when the body reaches ${40}^{∘}\text{C}.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T({t}_{1}) & =40 \\ 34+Ke^{-k{t}_{1}} & =40 \\ Ke^{-k{t}_{1}} & =6 \\ e^{-k{t}_{1}} & =\frac{6}{K} \\ -k{t}_{1} & =\ln\left(\frac{6}{K}\right) \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{k}\ln\left(\frac{6}{K}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute the values of $K$ and $k$ to obtain the time measured since cooling began:

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{29}{52} \right)}}{4}}\ln\left(\frac{6}{52\left(\frac{52}{29}\right)^{\frac{1}{4}}}\right) \\ {t}_{1} & =1+4\frac{\ln(\frac{3}{26})}{\ln(\frac{29}{52})}≈16\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

generation.domain: T(t)>ambient; positive rate; t>=0; observations strictly cooling
